questions.problem: Factor the expression $2{r}^{4}-32.$
questions.worked_solution:
The difference of squares formula is given by

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that all of the terms in our expression have a common factor of $2.$ To simplify the computation, we can factor out the $2,$ as follows:

$$
2{r}^{4}-32=2\cdot {r}^{4}-2\cdot 16=2({r}^{4}-16)
$$

The expression in parentheses can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
2({r}^{4}-16)=2({({r}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
2({({r}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})=2({r}^{2}+4)({r}^{2}-4)
$$

Finally, we notice that the expression in the second set of parentheses is also a difference of squares. Therefore, the expression can be factored further, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2({r}^{2}+4)({r}^{2}-4) & =2({r}^{2}+4)({r}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =2({r}^{2}+4)(r+2)(r-2)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Terms of a Fibonacci Sequence Given in Function Notation
questions.problem:
The recursive formula for the Fibonacci numbers is 

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n),\,f(1)=f(2)=1,\,n\ge 1.
$$

The $6$th term of the sequence is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The recursion relation is

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n).
$$

Substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =1+1 \\ f(3) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, substituting $n=2,3,4$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & =f(2+2)=f(2+1)+f(2)=f(3)+f(2)=2+1=3 \\ f(5) & =f(3+2)=f(3+1)+f(3)=f(4)+f(3)=3+2=5 \\ f(6) & =f(4+2)=f(4+1)+f(4)=f(5)+f(4)=5+3=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $6$th term of the sequence is $8.$

questions.problem: Solve the equation $\,{x}^{2}+2x=-50.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form by bringing all of the terms to the left-hand side. This gives the equation

$$
{x}^{2}+2x+50=0.
$$

We can find the roots of a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:

$$
x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}
$$

In this case, the coefficients are $a=1,\,b=2,$ and $c=50.$ Substituting these values into the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{{2}^{2}-4(1)(50)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{4-200}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{-196}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm 14\,\text{i}}{2} \\  & =-1\pm 7\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=-1+7\,\text{i}$ and $x=-1-7\,\text{i}.$

questions.problem: The multiplicity of the root $x=-5$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-15x-100$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=-5$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x+5)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x+5)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x+5)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+5)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-5$ | $1$ | $6$ | $-15$ | $-100$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-5$ | $-5$ | $100$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ | $-20$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x+5}={x}^{2}+x-20,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x+5)({x}^{2}+x-20).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x+5)(x-4)(x+5) \\  & =(x-4)(x+5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x+5)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-5$ has multiplicity $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+32x+16 \\  & ={x}^{2}(2x+1)+16(2x+1) \\  & =({x}^{2}+16)(2x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the factor $({x}^{2}+16)$ cannot be factored any further, and it does not have any real roots.

The only real root of $p(x)$ comes from the factor $(2x+1).$ This factor has a root of $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ and the exponent of the factor is $1.$ Therefore, the root $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, there is no root with multiplicity $2.$

The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Terms of a Fibonacci Sequence Given in Function Notation
questions.worked_solution:
The recursion relation is

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n).
$$

Substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =5+0 \\ f(3) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $n=2$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+2) & =f(2+1)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =f(3)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =5+5 \\ f(4) & =10\end{aligned}
$$

We continue this process to compute $f(5)$ and $f(6)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5) & =f(3+2)=f(3+1)+f(3)=f(4)+f(3)=10+5=15 \\ f(6) & =f(4+2)=f(4+1)+f(4)=f(5)+f(4)=15+10=25\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(6)=25.$

$$
{x}^{2}-6x+13=0.
$$

We can find the roots of a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:

$$
x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}
$$

In this case, the coefficients are $a=1,\,b=-6,$ and $c=13.$ Substituting these values into the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-(-6)\pm \sqrt{(-6)^{2}-4(1)(13)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{6\pm \sqrt{36-52}}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\pm \sqrt{-16}}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\pm 4\,\text{i}}{2} \\  & =3\pm 2\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=3+2\,\text{i}$ and $x=3-2\,\text{i}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Rule of Product
questions.problem: How many possible outcomes are there if a coin is flipped twice, a six-sided die is rolled three times, and a tetrahedral (four-sided) die is rolled once?
questions.worked_solution:
For the coin, there are $2$ outcomes: "Heads" and "Tails".

For the six-sided die, there is a total of $6$ outcomes: $1,2,3,4,5,6.$

For the tetrahedral die, there is a total of $4$ outcomes: $1,2,3,4.$

Using the **rule of product**, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Possible Outcomes} & =\text{Number of outcomes when the coin is flipped the first time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the coin is flipped the second time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the first time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the second time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the third time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the tetrahedral die is rolled the one time} \\  & =2\times 2\times 6\times 6\times 6\times 4 \\  & ={2}^{2}\times {6}^{3}\times 4 \\  & =4\times 216\times 4 \\  & =3\,456.\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are $3\,456$ possible outcomes.

questions.knowledge_point: Counting the Number of Possible Rational Roots of a Polynomial
questions.problem: According to the rational root theorem, the polynomial $f(x)=25{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-x-5$ has{{field-1}} *potential* rational roots.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $-5,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 5.$

- The leading coefficient is $25,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$, $\pm 5$, and $\pm 25.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1},\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{5},\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{25}, \\ \pm \frac{5}{1},\text{ }\pm \frac{5}{5},\text{ }\pm \frac{5}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to their lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1,\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{5},\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{25}, \\ \pm 5,\text{ }\pm 1,\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that some potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{25},\,\pm \frac{1}{5},\,\pm 1,\,\pm 5.
$$

This makes a total of $8$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 4=8.$)

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Cubic Polynomial Using the Rational Roots Theorem
questions.problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x)=27{x}^{3}-54{x}^{2}+36x-8$ has a root in the interval $(\frac{1}{2},1),$ the sum of the **distinct** real roots of $f(x)$ equals{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-8$ and the leading coefficient is $27.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-8}{\text{factor of }27}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \pm \frac{1}{27},\,\pm \frac{2}{27},\,\pm \frac{1}{9},\,\pm \frac{4}{27},\,\pm \frac{2}{9},\,\frac{8}{27},\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{4}{9}, \\  & \pm \frac{2}{3},\,\pm \frac{8}{9},\,\pm 1,\,\pm \frac{4}{3},\,\pm 2,\,\pm \frac{8}{3},\,\pm 4,\,\pm 8\end{aligned}
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(\frac{1}{2},1)$ are $\frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{8}{9}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-\frac{2}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\frac{2}{3}$ | $27$ | $-54$ | $36$ | $-8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $18$ | $-24$ | $8$ |
|  | $27$ | $-36$ | $12$ | $0$ |

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{2}{3})(27{x}^{2}-36x+12).\end{aligned}
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{2}{3})(27{x}^{2}-36x+12) \\  & =3(x-\frac{2}{3})(9{x}^{2}-12x+4) \\  & =3(x-\frac{2}{3})(3x-2)^{2} \\  & =(3x-2)(3x-2)^{2} \\  & =(3x-2)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only root of $f(x)$ is $x=\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-10x+8$ has one of its roots in the interval $(-5,-1),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $8$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }8}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 4,\pm 8
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-5,-1),$ are $-4$ and $-2.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |

| $-4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-10$ | $8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-4$ | $12$ | $-8$ |
|  | $1$ | $-3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+4)({x}^{2}-3x+2) \\  & =(x+4)(x-1)(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-4,1,2.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-4+1+2=-1.
$$

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-24}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 8,\,\pm 12,\,\pm 24.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-3)({x}^{2}+6x+8) \\  & =(x-3)(x+2)(x+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find that, in ascending order, the roots of the polynomial are $x=-4,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=3.$

questions.problem: If $\frac{p-2}{p+2}+X=\frac{2p}{3p+6},$ then what is $X?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $\frac{p-2}{p+2}+X=\frac{2p}{3p+6},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\frac{2p}{3p+6}-\frac{p-2}{p+2} \\  & =\frac{2p}{3(p+2)}-\frac{p-2}{p+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to add the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. Here, we can put both fractions over a common denominator of $3(p+2)$ if we multiply the top and bottom of the second fraction by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\frac{2p}{3(p+2)}-\frac{p-2}{p+2} \\  & =\frac{2p}{3(p+2)}-\frac{3}{3}\cdot \frac{p-2}{p+2} \\  & =\frac{2p}{3(p+2)}-\frac{3(p-2)}{3(p+2)} \\  & =\frac{2p-3(p-2)}{3(p+2)} \\  & =\frac{2p-3p+6}{3(p+2)} \\  & =\frac{-p+6}{3(p+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $X=\frac{-p+6}{3(p+2)}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Two-Step Equations
questions.worked_solution:
In part 1, we found that $p(20)=400a+20b.$ So, we need to solve the equation $400a+20b=4\,800$ for the parameter $b.$

We need to isolate the variable $b.$ To do this, we treat $a$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we subtract $400a$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}400a+20b & =4\,800 \\ 400a+20b-400a & =4\,800-400a \\ 20b & =4\,800-400a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}20b & =4\,800-400a \\ \frac{20b}{20} & =\frac{4\,800-400a}{20} \\ \frac{\cancel{20}b}{\cancel{20}} & =\frac{4\,800}{20}-\frac{400a}{20} \\ b & =240-20a\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $b=240-20a.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
We have the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=240-20a \\ 30b+900a=6\,000\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=240-20a
$$

So, we replace $b$ in the second equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}30b+900a & =6\,000 \\ 30(240-20a)+900a & =6\,000 \\ 7\,200-600a+900a & =6\,000 \\ 7\,200+300a & =6\,000 \\ 300a & =-1\,200 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $a=-4$ into $b=240-20a,$ we can then find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =240-20(-4) \\ b & =320\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-4,\,b=320.$

We factor $4{x}^{2}-320x+6\,000$ using the greatest common factor (GCF).

Computing the GCF, we get

$$
\text{GCF}(4{x}^{2},320x,6\,000)=4
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-320x+6\,000 & = \\ 4\cdot ({x}^{2})+4\cdot (-80x)+4\cdot (1\,500)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot ({x}^{2})+4\cdot (-80x)+4\cdot (1\,500) & = \\ 4({x}^{2}-80x+1\,500)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${x}^{2}-80x+1\,500.$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring Trinomials With Positive Coefficients
questions.problem:
Find the minimum number of cakes the bakery needs to produce per week to make a weekly profit of $$6\,000.$

The bakery needs to produce$\,$
{{field-1}}$\,$ cakes per week.
questions.worked_solution:
From part 5, the required number of cakes $x$ is the solution to the equation

$$
4\cdot ({x}^{2}-80x+1\,500)=0.
$$

Dividing this equation by $4,$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}-80x+1\,500=0.
$$

To solve this equation, we want to find a factor pair of the constant term $(1\,500)$ that also adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-80).$ The required factors are $(-30)$ and $(-50).$

Using this factor pair, we write the linear term as $-80x=-30x-50x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-80x+1\,500 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-30x-50x+1\,500 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-30x-50x+1\,500 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-30x)+(-50x+1\,500) & =0 \\ x(x-30)-50(x-30) & =0 \\ (x-30)(x-50)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the solutions are $x=30$ or $x=50.$ Since we require the minimum solution, we conclude that the bakery needs to produce $30$ cakes per week to make a profit of $$6\,000.$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting a Recursive Formula to an Explicit Formula
questions.problem:
The bakery wants to increase its output by implementing a new production model. The number of cakes ${a}_{n}$ produced in the $n$th week since the implementation of the new model is given by the arithmetic sequence

$$
{a}_{n+1}={a}_{n}+4,\,{a}_{1}=19,\,n\ge 1
$$

What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence?

${a}_{n}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,\,n\ge 1,
$$

so we need to determine the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is ${a}_{1}=19,$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+4 \\  & =19+4 \\  & =23\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =23-19 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute ${a}_{1}=19$ and $d=4$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =19+(n-1)(4) \\  & =19+4n-4 \\  & =4n+15\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=4n+15,\,n\ge 1.
$$

questions.problem: Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+7}{5-x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=\frac{3x+7}{5-x}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=\frac{3y+7}{5-y}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{3y+7}{5-y} \\ x(5-y) & =3y+7 \\ 5x-xy & =3y+7 \\ 5x-7 & =3y+xy \\ 5x-7 & =y(x+3) \\ y & =\frac{5x-7}{x+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{5x-7}{x+3}.
$$

questions.problem: Factor $8{z}^{4}-128$ completely.
questions.worked_solution:
The difference of squares formula is given by

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that all of the terms in our expression have a common factor of $8.$ To simplify the computation, we can factor out the $8,$ as follows:

$$
8{z}^{4}-128=8\cdot {z}^{4}-8\cdot 16=8({z}^{4}-16)
$$

The expression in parentheses can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
8({z}^{4}-16)=8({({z}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
8({({z}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})=8({z}^{2}+4)({z}^{2}-4)
$$

Finally, we notice that the expression in the second set of parentheses is also a difference of squares. Therefore, the expression can be factored further, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8({z}^{2}+4)({z}^{2}-4) & =8({z}^{2}+4)({z}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =8({z}^{2}+4)(z+2)(z-2)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What are the solutions of the equation $(x+3)^{2}=-4?$
questions.worked_solution:
The left-hand side is a perfect square. Therefore, we can solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =-4 \\ x+3 & =\pm \sqrt{-4} \\ x+3 & =\pm 2\,\text{i} \\ x & =-3\pm 2\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=-3+2\,\text{i}$ and $x=-3-2\,\text{i}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Relating a Derivative to a Rate of Change
questions.problem:
To measure the success of an amusement park, Ed uses the following three functions that model the daily number of visitors to the park $t$ minutes after the park is opened to the public.

- $N(t)$ - the number of people inside the park

- $E(t)$ - the rate at which people enter the park

- $L(t)$ - the rate at which people leave the park

What is the relationship between the functions above?
questions.worked_solution:
The function $N(t)$ gives the number of people inside the park $t$ minutes after opening. Then,

$$
{N}^{'}(t)=\frac{\text{d}N(t)}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{Change in }N}{\text{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, ${N}^{'}(t)$ gives the rate at which the number of people inside the park changes $t$ minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the park at time $t$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $t.$ That is,

$$
{N}^{'}(t)=E(t)-L(t).
$$

$$

questions.problem:
What is the index of the term $192$ for the geometric sequence below?

$$
f(n+1)=2f(n),\,f(1)=3,\,n\ge 1
$$
questions.worked_solution:
This geometric sequence is given as a recurrence relation, i.e.,

$$
f(n+1)=r\cdot f(n).
$$

Therefore:

$$
f(1)=3,\,r=2.
$$

We're interested in finding $n$ such that $f(n)=192.$ Using the formula for the $n$th term, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ 192 & =3\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\ \frac{192}{3} & ={2}^{n-1} \\ 64 & ={2}^{n-1} \\ {2}^{6} & ={2}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the exponents gives:

$$
6=n-1\,⟹\,n=7
$$

Therefore, $192$ is the $7$th term of the sequence.

questions.problem: What is $\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})$ expressed in terms of a reference angle?
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to express $\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})$ in terms of $\operatorname{tan}{\theta }_{R},$ where ${\theta }_{R}$ is the reference angle corresponding to the angle $\theta =-\frac{17\pi }{12}.$ 

To express $\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})$ in terms of $\operatorname{tan}{\theta }_{R},$ we proceed as follows: 

- **Step 1**: Find the corresponding coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$ We do this by adding integer multiples of $2\pi $ until we get our desired angle:

$$
-\frac{17\pi }{12}+2\pi =\frac{7\pi }{12}\,✓
$$

Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})=\operatorname{tan}(\frac{7\pi }{12}).
$$

$$
{\theta }_{R}=\pi -\frac{7\pi }{12}=\frac{5\pi }{12}.
$$

- **Step 3**: Determine the correct sign. The tangent function is negative $(-)$ in the second quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})=-\operatorname{tan}{\theta }_{R}=-\operatorname{tan}(\frac{5\pi }{12})
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})=-\operatorname{tan}(\frac{5\pi }{12}).
$$

rounded to the nearest tenth.

questions.problem: Given that $-2{x}^{2}-4kx-8k=0,$ where $k$ is a **positive** constant, has exactly one real solution, what is the value of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
A quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is equal to zero: $D=0.$

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

$$
a=-2,\,b=-4k,\,c=-8k
$$

So, computing the discriminant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(-4k)^{2}-4(-2)(-8k) \\  & =16{k}^{2}-64k.\end{aligned}
$$

To have exactly one real solution, we need $D=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}16{k}^{2}-64k & =0 \\ 16k(k-4) & =0 \\ k & =0,4\end{aligned}
$$

Since $k$ must be positive, we conclude that $k=4.$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying Several Transformations: Horizontal Stretch Followed By Horizontal Shift Inside Parentheses
questions.problem:
Given the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following transformations in the order given:

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $8$ parallel to the $y$-axis

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $x$-axis

- Translate it to the left by $10$ units

What is the final function expression after applying all the transformations?
questions.worked_solution:
To find the expression, let's apply each of the transformations in turn.

- Stretching the graph of $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $8$ parallel to the $y$-axis is equivalent to multiplying the function expression by $8.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

$$
y=8f(x).
$$

- Stretching the graph of $y=8f(x)$ by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $x$-axis is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $\frac{1}{5}x.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

$$
y=8f(\frac{1}{5}x)=8f(\frac{x}{5}).
$$

- Translating the graph of $y=8f(\frac{x}{5})$ by $10$ units to the left is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $(x+10).$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

$$
y=8f(\frac{1}{5}(x+10))=8f(\frac{x}{5}+2).
$$

Therefore, the final function expression is $y=8f(\frac{x}{5}+2).$

questions.worked_solution:
The recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+2}={a}_{n+1}+{a}_{n}.
$$

Substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1+2} & ={a}_{1+1}+{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{2}+{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{3} & =6+1 \\ {a}_{3} & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $n=2$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2+2} & ={a}_{2+1}+{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{3}+{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{4} & =7+6 \\ {a}_{4} & =13\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${a}_{4}=13.$

questions.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $(2,5)$ and the line $3y+2x=6.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the equation of the given line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y+2x & =6 \\ 3y & =-2x+6 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Let's draw a diagram describing our situation.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/q-74437-e-0)

Next, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=-\frac{2}{3}x+2$ and passes through the point $(2,5).$

 The given line has a slope of $-\frac{2}{3},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $\frac{3}{2}.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5 & =\frac{3}{2}(x-2) \\ y-5 & =\frac{3}{2}x-3 \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-\frac{2}{3}x+2 \\ y=\frac{3}{2}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}x+2 & =\frac{3}{2}x+2 \\ -\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{3}{2}x & =2-2 \\ -\frac{13}{6}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$ into either of the two equations gives $y=2.$ So, our solution is $x=0$ and $y=2.$ So, the lines intersect at the point $(0,2).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(2,5)$ and $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(0-2)}^{2}+(2-5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+9} \\  & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the shortest distance between the point $(2,5)$ and the line $3y+2x=6$ is $\sqrt{13}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}(9{m}^{2}+{n}^{2})(9{m}^{2}-{n}^{2}) & =(9{m}^{2}+{n}^{2})(3m+n)(3m-n)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Is the function $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-2x$ even, odd, or neither?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

- a function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$ for all $x$

- a function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$

Computing $f(-x)$ for the given function and comparing it to $f(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =2(-x)^{3}-2(-x) \\  & =-2{x}^{3}+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)\ne f(x),$ the function is not even.

Lastly, we compute $-f(x)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}-f(x) & =-(2{x}^{3}-2x) \\  & =-2{x}^{3}+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)=-f(x),$ the function is odd.

questions.worked_solution:
To construct the formula for the sequence, we need to know the common difference $d$ and the first term ${a}_{1}.$

Since we are given ${a}_{4}=13$ and ${a}_{8}=41,$ we can find the common difference by dividing the total difference by the number of jumps:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{8}-{a}_{4}}{8-4} \\  & =\frac{41-13}{8-4} \\  & =\frac{28}{4} \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${a}_{4}=13$ is $3$ jumps after ${a}_{1},$ we can determine the first term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}+3d \\ 13 & ={a}_{1}+3(7) \\ 13 & ={a}_{1}+21 \\ -8 & ={a}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =-8+(n-1)(7) \\  & =-8+7n-7 \\  & =7n-15\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for the value of $n$ that gives ${a}_{n}=90,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =7n-15 \\ 90 & =7n-15 \\ 105 & =7n \\ \frac{105}{7} & =n \\ 15 & =n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $90$ is the $15$th term of the sequence.

questions.problem:
If $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are polynomials of degree $3$ and $7,$ respectively, which of the following statements are true?

I. - $P+Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $10$
II. - $P-Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $4$
III. - $P\cdot Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $10$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, suppose $P(x)={x}^{3}$ and $Q(x)={x}^{7}.$ Then $P+Q={x}^{3}+{x}^{7},$ which is not a polynomial of degree $10.$

- Statement II is false. For example, suppose $P(x)={x}^{3}$ and $Q(x)={x}^{7}.$ Then $P-Q={x}^{3}-{x}^{7},$ which is not a polynomial of degree $4.$

- Statement III is true. The highest-degree terms in $P$ and $Q$ must contain ${x}^{3}$ and ${x}^{7},$ respectively. Therefore, the highest-degree term in $P\cdot Q$ must contain ${x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{7}={x}^{3+7}={x}^{10},$ meaning that $P\cdot Q$ has degree $10.$

In conclusion, only statement III is true.

Given that $f(x)=|x-4|+2,$ on which of the following intervals is $f(x)$ invertible?

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on any of the intervals $x\in (1,\infty )$  and $(-\infty ,5].$ On each of these intervals, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

$$

Therefore,

$$
k-c=4-(-3)=7.
$$

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by $\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi }.$ This gives

$$

questions.problem: Given that $m\ge 0$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{m(m+1)!}{(m+2)!}.$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Reciprocal Ratio of a Quadrantal Angle
questions.problem: Find the value of $\operatorname{sec}0+\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
The angles $0$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/q-123586-e-0)

- Let's first consider the angle $0.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $0$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$  Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}0=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}0=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}0}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

- Now, let's consider the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$  Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{sec}0+\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1+1=2.
$$

questions.problem: What is the multiplicity of the root $x=4$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+32?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=4$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-4)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $4$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $0$ | $32$ |
|  | $↓$ | $4$ | $-8$ | $-32$ |
|  | $1$ | $-2$ | $-8$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-4}={x}^{2}-2x-8,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-4)({x}^{2}-2x-8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-4)(x+2)(x-4) \\  & =(x+2)(x-4)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-4)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=4$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following expressions are **irrational**?

I. - ${8}^{5}\cdot \sqrt{36}$
II. - ${3}^{20}\cdot 7.0523$
III. - $\sqrt{2}\cdot {2}^{-15}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- the product of two rational numbers is *always* rational:

$$
\text{rational}\times \text{rational}=\text{rational}
$$

- the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is *always* irrational:

$$
\text{rational}\times \text{irrational}=\text{irrational}
$$

- the product of two irrational numbers is *sometimes* rational and *sometimes* irrational.

With that in mind, let's examine the statements.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{5}^{x}-1-(\operatorname{ln}5)x}{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}5} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[{5}^{x}-1-(\operatorname{ln}5)x]}^{'}}{[{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}5]^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\operatorname{ln}5)\cdot {5}^{x}-(\operatorname{ln}5)}{2\operatorname{ln}5\cdot x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{5}^{x}-1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{5}^{x}-1-(\operatorname{ln}5)x}{{x}^{2}\text{ }\operatorname{ln}5} & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{5}^{x}-1}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[{5}^{x}-1]}^{'}}{[x]^{'}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\operatorname{ln}5){5}^{x}}{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,(\operatorname{ln}5){e}^{0} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The displacement $s$ (in meters) relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by the equation $s(t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6}{{t}^{2}+1}$, where $t$ is the time, measured in seconds. Find the position ${s}_{0}$ and velocity ${v}_{0}$ of the particle at the initial moment of time $t=0\,\text{s}.$

${s}_{0}=$
{{field-1}}$\text{m}\,\text{and}\,$
${v}_{0}=$
{{field-2}}$\text{m/s}$

To calculate the initial position, we substitute $t=0$ it into the equation $s(t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6}{{t}^{2}+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{0} & =s(0) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}(0+1)+6}{{0}^{2}+1} \\  & =6\,\text{m}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6}{{t}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{t+1}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)-(\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6)\cdot 2t}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+1-2t(t+1)(\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6)}{(t+1)({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the velocity at $t=0\,\text{s},$ we substitute $t=0$ into the velocity function above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(0) \\  & =\frac{{0}^{2}+1-2(0)(0+1)(\operatorname{ln}(0+1)+6)}{(0+1)({0}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot {1}^{2}} \\  & =1\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/q-343501)

A spherical balloon is being inflated so that its volume is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the balloon is changing with respect to the radius at the moment when the diameter of the balloon is equal to $18\,\text{cm}.$

The instantaneous rate of change at the moment when the diameter is $18$ centimeters is equal to
{{field-1}} ${\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{cm}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the diameter of the spherical balloon is $18\,\text{cm}$, its radius $r$ is $9\,\text{cm}.$ Now, the volume of a sphere with radius $r$ is given by 

$$
V=V(r)=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $V(r)$ with respect to $r$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{'}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\pi (3{r}^{2}) \\  & =4\pi {r}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $r=9$ gives

$$
{V}^{'}(9)=4\pi (9)^{2}=324\pi .
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at which the volume of the balloon is increasing when the diameter is $18\,\text{cm}$ is $324\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{cm}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Substituting $t=\pi $ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}v(t) & ={lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}4{csc}^{2}(t) \\  & =4{csc}^{2}(\pi ) \\  & =4\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}(\pi )} \\  & =\frac{4}{{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{csc}t.$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/ed5d88921baeae6aa1e3771182a8c07b)

As $t$ approaches $\pi $ from the left, the values of $y=\operatorname{csc}t$ are positive and grow without bound. 

Therefore

$$
{lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{csc}t=\infty 
$$

Applying the product and power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}4{csc}^{2}(t) & ={lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}4\cdot {lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}{csc}^{2}(t) \\  & =4\cdot {({lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{csc}(t))}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
4\cdot {({lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{csc}(t))}^{2}=\infty .

questions.problem:

Now, we see that $v(t)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}=8u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{'}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t} \\  & =8u\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =(8\operatorname{csc}t)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =-8{csc}^{2}t\operatorname{cot}t.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

questions.problem: The number of computers affected by the spread of some ransomware after $t$ days can be modeled by the function $f(t)=\frac{100\,({t}^{3}+2)}{t+1}.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change in the number of infected computers when $t=9$ days?
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change in the spread when $t=9$ days is equal to ${f}^{'}(9).$ 

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{100\,({t}^{3}+2)}{t+1}) \\  & =\frac{100(3{t}^{2})(t+1)-100({t}^{3}+2)(1)}{{(t+1)}^{2}} \\  & =100\cdot \frac{2{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}-2}{{(t+1)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change in the spread when $t=9$ is $1\,699$ computers per day.

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral
questions.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{-\pi }^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{cos}^{2}(-\pi +\frac{\pi k}{n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{n}].$
questions.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=-\pi .$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{\pi }{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{\pi }{n}=\frac{b-(-\pi )}{n}\,⟹\,b=0.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=-\pi +\frac{\pi k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})={cos}^{2}{x}_{k}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{0}{cos}^{2}x\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{cos}^{2}(-\pi +\frac{\pi k}{n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)={cos}^{2}x$ and $b=0.$

If we attempt to evaluate the limit directly by substituting $x=2,$ we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2}}{2x-{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}}{2(2)-(2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since there is a radical in the numerator, we can evaluate the limit by first multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2}}{2x-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})}{(2x-{x}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{x-2}{x(2-x)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{-(2-x)}{x(2-x)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{\cancel{2-x}}{x\cancel{(2-x)}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{1}{x(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate ${lim}_{x\to \pi /3}\operatorname{csc}(3x).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's attempt to evaluate the limit by direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /3}\operatorname{csc}(3x) & =\operatorname{csc}(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{csc}(\pi ) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}(\pi )} \\  & =\frac{1}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{csc}(3x).$

![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/q-47042-e-0)

As $x$ approaches $\frac{\pi }{3}$ from the left, the values of $y=\operatorname{csc}(3x)$ are positive and grow without bound. So,

$$
{lim}_{x\to (\pi /3)^{-}}\operatorname{csc}(3x)=\infty .
$$

Similarly, as $x$ approaches $\frac{\pi }{3}$ from the right, the values of $y=\operatorname{csc}(3x)$ are negative and decrease without bound. So,

$$
{lim}_{x\to (\pi /3)^{+}}\operatorname{csc}(3x)=-\infty .
$$

Therefore, since the two limits are not equal, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \pi /3}\operatorname{csc}(3x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{sin}2x.$ Then

$$
{u}^{'}(x)=2x,\,{v}^{'}(x)=2\operatorname{cos}2x.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x) \\  & =(2x)(\operatorname{sin}2x)+({x}^{2})(2\operatorname{cos}2x) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}2x+2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})|}_{x=\pi /4} \\  & =2(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot \operatorname{sin}(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+2{(\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}\operatorname{cos}(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})+2\cdot \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}\cdot \operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/q-73174)

The area under the curve $y=4-{x}^{2}$ between $x=-2$, $x=1$ and the $x$-axis is approximated using a right Riemann sum, as shown above. What is the expression for the Riemann sum in sigma notation?
questions.worked_solution:
The right Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ with $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

From the diagram, we see that there are $n=3$ rectangles. The endpoints indicate that $a=-2$ and $b=1,$ so the step size is 

$$
Δx=\frac{1-(-2)}{3}=\frac{3}{3}=1.
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the right Riemann sum can be expressed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f(a+iΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}f(-2+i\cdot 1)\cdot 1 \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}f(i-2) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}[4-(i-2)^{2}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}[4-({i}^{2}-4i+4)] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}[4i-{i}^{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 1:** First, we write the inverse function implicitly. The given function is $y=3\operatorname{tan}(2x-1),$ and to write the inverse function implicitly, we swap $x$ and $y$ as follows:

$$

$$

Note that in the equation above, we have $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

**Step 2:** Next, we differentiate. The overall goal is to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ but the equation is already solved for $x,$ so we compute $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}$ and then take the reciprocal:

$$

$$

$$

questions.problem: The equation of a curve is $3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}=9.$ The normal line at the point $(3,\,3)$ intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(3,\,3).$  Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{'},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 6x-4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-6x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-6x}{-4y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3x}{2y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(3,\,3)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & ={(\frac{3x}{2y})}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 3}{2\cdot 3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is ${m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3/2}=-\frac{2}{3}.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(3,\,3)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{'}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-3) & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3) \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{'}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4\sqrt{x+4}-x-8}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+4}}-1]}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+4}}-1]}^{'}}{[2x]^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[-\frac{1}{(x+4)\sqrt{x+4}}]}{2} \\  & =\frac{[-\frac{1}{(0+4)\sqrt{0+4}}]}{2} \\  & =\frac{[-\frac{1}{4(2)}]}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Research of a factory assembly line shows that the number of units $f$ produced in $x$ hours can be modeled by the function $f(x)={x}^{2}+20x.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of production when $x=2$ hours?

The instantaneous rate of change of production when $x=2$ hours is equal to ${f}^{'}(2).$

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+20x) \\  & =2x+20.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(2) & =2(2)+20 \\  & =4+20 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of production when $x=2$ hours is $24$ units per hour.

questions.problem:
![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/q-2545)

The area $A$ of the circle above is increasing. The circumference and radius of the circle are $C$ and $r$ respectively. 
Find the rate of change of the area of the circle with respect to its circumference.
questions.worked_solution:
The area of a circle is given by

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2},
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the circle.

We know that $C=2\pi r.$ so we can express the area $A$ as a function of the circumference $C$ by substituting $r=\frac{C}{2\pi }$ in the formula above. We get

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $A(C)$ with respect to $C$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{'}(C) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\  & =\frac{1}{4\pi }\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}({C}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4\pi }(2C) \\  & =\frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.problem: Find the slope of $y=\operatorname{sin}({x}^{2}+2x-1)$ at $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is given by ${f}^{'}(0).$

We will calculate ${f}^{'}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}u,\,u={x}^{2}+2x-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot (2x+2) \\  & =(2x+2)\operatorname{cos}u \\  & =(2x+2)\operatorname{cos}({x}^{2}+2x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+2)\operatorname{cos}({0}^{2}+2\cdot 0-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}(-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is $2\operatorname{cos}1.$

Find where the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt[4]{x}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt[4]{x}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{x}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{'}(1)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{1}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=-2.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-2\cdot (x-1) \\ y & =-2x+2+2 \\ y & =-2x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+4 & =0 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,2,0\,).$

questions.worked_solution:
Applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{2x+8}{\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{4}+5}}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to -1}(2x+8)}{{lim}_{x\to -1}\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{4}+5}}\,.
$$

We calculate the limits of the numerator and the denominator separately.

For the numerator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}(2x+8) & =2{lim}_{x\to -1}x+{lim}_{x\to -1}8 \\  & =2(-1)+8 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the root rule in the denominator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{4}+5} & =\sqrt[3]{{lim}_{x\to -1}(3{x}^{4}+5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{3(-1)^{4}+5} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{8} \\  & =2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{2x+8}{\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{4}+5}} & =\frac{6}{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](https://mathacademy.com/graphics/q-142991)

The function $h$ is a part of the graph of the function $y=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3,$ as shown in the figure above. Find the number of weeks $x$ at which the stock price given by this function was $$5,000.$

*Hint: Remember that $h$ is measured in thousands of dollars.*

questions.worked_solution:
We have to solve $h(x)=5,$ or equivalently, $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3=5.$

First, we isolate the term $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}$ by subtracting $3$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3 & =5 \\ \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we isolate the square root by multiplying by $\frac{3}{2}$ on both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x} & =2 \\ \sqrt{x} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the square root is isolated, we can proceed as usual. Squaring both sides of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =3 \\ (\sqrt{x})^{2} & ={3}^{2} \\ x & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check the result by plugging it into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{9}+3 & \overset{?}{=}5 \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot 3+3 & \overset{?}{=}5 \\ 2+3 & =5\,\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The value $x=9$ satisfies the original equation, so we can accept it as a solution.

Therefore, the solution to $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3=5$  is $x=9.$

$$

The left Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{S}_{L}={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})Δx,
$$

$$

The area under the curve $y=\frac{x+1}{x}$ between $x=1$, $x=4$ and the $x$-axis is approximated using a left Riemann sum, as shown above. What is the expression for the Riemann sum in sigma notation?
questions.worked_solution:
The left Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ with $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

From the diagram, we see that there are $n=3$ rectangles. The endpoints indicate that $a=1$ and $b=4,$ so the step size is

$$
Δx=\frac{4-1}{3}=\frac{3}{3}=1.
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the left Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})Δx & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(a+kΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{3-1}f(1+k\cdot 1)\cdot 1 \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{2}f(1+k) \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{2}\frac{1+k+1}{1+k} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{2}\frac{2+k}{1+k}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The area under the curve $y={e}^{x+2}$ between $x=-2$ and $x=2$ and the $x$-axis is approximated by a left Riemann sum using $8$ subintervals of equal length. What is the expression for the left Riemann sum ${S}_{L}$ in sigma notation?

*Hint: Write down the expression in terms of $j.$*

${S}_{L}=\frac{1}{2}$
${\sum }_{j=0}^{7}$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The left Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{S}_{L}={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx$ with $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

We're given that there are  $n=8$ subintervals.  The endpoints indicate that $a=-2$ and $b=2,$  so the step size is 

$$
Δx=\frac{2-(-2)}{8}=\frac{4}{8}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the left Riemann sum ${S}_{L}$ can be expressed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{L}={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})Δx & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f(a+jΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{8-1}f(-2+j\cdot \frac{1}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{7}f(-2+\frac{j}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{j=0}^{7}{e}^{((-2+j/2)+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{j=0}^{7}{e}^{j/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(2{y}^{2}+7y-\frac{3}{y}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(2{y}^{2}+7y-3{y}^{-1}) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})+7\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y)-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{-1}) \\  & =4y+7+3{y}^{-2} \\  & =4y+7+\frac{3}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{y}^{3}+7{y}^{2}+3}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{4{y}^{3}+7{y}^{2}+3}.
$$

questions.problem: Given a curve $x=6{y}^{2}+2y-5,$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(3,1)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(6{y}^{2}+2y-5) \\  & =6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y)-5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =6\cdot (2y)+2(1)+0 \\  & =12y+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{12y+2}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(3,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(3,1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{12\cdot 1+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-3) \\ y & =\frac{x}{14}-\frac{3}{14}+1 \\ y & =\frac{x}{14}+\frac{11}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2y-3\sqrt{y}}.

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-0) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+4.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}8x-1}{2x}.$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}8x}{8x} & =-4\cdot 0=0.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: What is ${\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{x},$ the lower bound is $a=4$ and the upper bound is $b=9.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{9-4}{n}=\frac{5}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(4+k\cdot \frac{5}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(4+\frac{5k}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\sqrt{4+\frac{5k}{n}}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the downward-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(2,4)$ and which passes through the point $(4,1).$

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k).
$$

Here, the vertex has coordinates $(h,k)=(2,4).$ Substituting these into the general standard equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =4p(y-4).\end{aligned}
$$

We are left to find the value of $p.$ We know that the given parabola also passes through the point $(4,1),$ so we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=1$ into the standard equation and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =4p(y-4) \\ (4-2)^{2} & =4p(1-4) \\ 4 & =-12p \\ p & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =4p(y-4) \\ (x-2)^{2} & =4(-\frac{1}{3})(y-4) \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-\frac{4}{3}(y-4).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(1) & =x \\ f(x) & =1 \\ 2x+\sqrt{x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{x} & =1-2x \\ x & =1-4x+4{x}^{2} \\ 4{x}^{2}-5x+1 & =0 \\ (4x-1)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =\frac{1}{4},\,1.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Let $f(x)$ be the function defined below. For what value of $k$ is $f(x)$ continuous at $x=-1?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{k}{x-1}, & x<-1 \\ 2x-k, & x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
From the definition of $f(x)$, the left-sided limit of $f(x)$ at $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}\frac{k}{x-1} \\  & =\frac{k}{-1-1} \\  & =-\frac{k}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}(2x-k) \\  & =2(-1)-k \\  & =-2-k.\end{aligned}
$$

We also note that $f(-1)=-2-k.$ 

So, for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}f(x) \\ -2-k & =-\frac{k}{2} \\ -4-2k & =-k \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=-4$ removes the discontinuity at $x=-1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Sum to Infinity of a Geometric Series Given Two of Its Terms
questions.worked_solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

From the question statement we have ${a}_{3}=27$ and ${a}_{6}=1.$ We can find the common ratio using the following formula:

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}
$$

Substituting in the known information into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{6-3} & =\frac{1}{27} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{1}{27} \\ {r}^{3} & ={(\frac{1}{3})}^{3} \\ r & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}{r}^{n-1}
$$

for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence, we can find the first term. Indeed, for $n=3$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}(r)^{2} \\ 27 & ={a}_{1}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2} \\ 27 & ={a}_{1}(\frac{1}{9}) \\ {a}_{1} & =243\end{aligned}
$$

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{243}{(1-\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =\frac{243}{(\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =243(\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\frac{729}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that  ${a}_{n}=2{n}^{5}$ for $n\ge 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. - $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1$
II. - ${a}_{n}$ is an increasing sequence
III. - ${a}_{n}$ is a decreasing sequence
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is a positive sequence defined for $n\ge 1,$ and that

$$
L=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}.
$$

Then,

- if $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *increasing,* and

- if $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *decreasing.*

Notice that, in this case, ${a}_{n}=2{n}^{5}$ is positive for all $n\ge 1.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement.

- Statement I is false. Computing the ratio $L,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}} \\  & =\frac{2(n+1)^{5}}{2{n}^{5}} \\  & =\frac{(n+1)^{5}}{{n}^{5}} \\  & ={(\frac{n+1}{n})}^{5} \\  & ={(\frac{n}{n}+\frac{1}{n})}^{5} \\  & ={(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $n\ge 1,$ we have that $\frac{1}{n}>0.$ Therefore, it follows that

$$
(1+\frac{1}{n})>1,
$$

and therefore 

$$
L={(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{5}>1.
$$

- Statement II is true whereas statement III is false. Since $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ we can conclude that the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is increasing.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Verifying Continuity at a Point Using the Definition
questions.problem:
Consider the following function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}-x-3, & x<-3 \\ 0, & x=-3 \\ x+3, & x>-3\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true regarding $f(x)?$

I. - $f(x)$ is defined at $x=-3$
II. - ${lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}f(x)$
III. - ${lim}_{x\to (-3)}f(x)=f(-3)$
IV. - $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-3$
questions.worked_solution:
To test for continuity of $f(x)$ at a point $x=c$, we need to check three conditions:

- Does $f(c)$ exist?

- Does ${lim}_{x\to c}f(x)$ exist?

- Does ${lim}_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)?$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Using the expression for the second branch of the function, we obtain that

$$
f(-3)=0.
$$

So, $f(x)$ is defined at $x=-3.$ $\,\,✓$

- Statement II is true. By calculating the one-sided limits, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}(-x-3) \\  & =-(-3)-3 \\  & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}(x+3) \\  & =(-3)+3 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

As a result:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}f(x)
$$

 
Therefore, the limit of $f(x)$ at $x=-3$ exists:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-3)}f(x)=0\,\,✓
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, we have that ${lim}_{x\to (-3)}f(x)=0=f(-3).$ $\,\,✓$

- Statement IV is true. Since all statements I-III are true, according to the continuity test, the function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true."

questions.problem: Find the equation of the midline for a transformed sine function with a minimum value of $0$ and a maximum value of $4.$

A sinusoidal graph's midline (or vertical shift) is the horizontal line that divides it vertically in half.

$$
y=\frac{{y}_{\text{min}}+{y}_{\text{max}}}{2},
$$

where ${y}_{\text{min}}$ and ${y}_{\text{max}}$ are the minimum and maximum values of the function. The midline equals the average of the maximum and minimum values.

$$

$$

Therefore, the midline is $y=2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Logarithmic Equations Containing a Constant on One Side
questions.problem: Solve the equation $\operatorname{log}(x-2)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{log}(256).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we use the power rule to simplify the right-hand side. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{log}(256) \\ \operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\operatorname{log}({256}^{1/4}) \\ \operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\operatorname{log}(4).\end{aligned}
$$

Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\operatorname{log}(4) \\ x-2 & =4 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation: 

- Substituting $x=6$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\operatorname{log}(6-2) \\  & =\operatorname{log}(4) \\  & =\operatorname{log}({256}^{1/4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{log}(256).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=6$ is a valid solution.

questions.problem: If ${log}_{3}(6-2x)=4{log}_{3}(\sqrt{3})$, then what is the value of $x?$

First, we use the power rule to simplify the right-hand side. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}(6-2x) & =4{log}_{3}(\sqrt{3}) \\ {log}_{3}(6-2x) & ={log}_{3}({(\sqrt{3})}^{4}) \\ {log}_{3}(6-2x) & ={log}_{3}(9).\end{aligned}
$$

Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}(6-2x) & ={log}_{3}(9) \\ 6-2x & =9 \\ 2x & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation: 

- Substituting $x=-\frac{3}{2}$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}(6-2x) & ={log}_{3}(6-2(-\frac{3}{2})) \\  & ={log}_{3}(6+3) \\  & ={log}_{3}(9) \\  & ={log}_{3}(\sqrt{3})^{4} \\  & =4{log}_{3}(\sqrt{3}).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-\frac{3}{2}$ is a valid solution.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Monotonic Polynomial and Rational Sequences
questions.problem:
Given that  ${a}_{n}=\frac{8}{n+4}$ for $n\ge 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. - $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1$
II. - ${a}_{n}$ is an increasing sequence
III. - ${a}_{n}$ is a decreasing sequence
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is a positive sequence defined for $n\ge 1,$ and that

$$
L=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}.
$$

Then,

- if $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *increasing,* and

- if $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *decreasing.*

Notice that, in this case, ${a}_{n}=\frac{8}{n+4}$ is positive for all $n\ge 1.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement.

- Statement I is false. Computing the ratio $L,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8}{n+5})}{(\frac{8}{n+4})} \\  & =\frac{8(n+4)}{8(n+5)} \\  & =\frac{n+4}{n+5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $n\ge 1,$ it follows that

$$
\frac{n+4}{n+5}<1,
$$

since the numerator is always smaller than the denominator. Therefore,

$$
0<L<1.
$$

- Statement II is false, whereas statement III is true. Since $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ we can conclude that the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{3} & ={e}^{3} \\ x & =3{e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $y=3{x}^{2}{({x}^{3}-1)}^{4}$, find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)=3{x}^{2}$ and $v(x)={({x}^{3}-1)}^{4}.$ Then

$$
{u}^{'}(x)=6x,\,{v}^{'}(x)=12{x}^{2}{({x}^{3}-1)}^{3}.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x) \\  & =(6x)(({x}^{3}-1)^{4})+(3{x}^{2})(12{x}^{2}({x}^{3}-1)^{3}) \\  & =6x({x}^{3}-1)^{4}+36{x}^{4}{({x}^{3}-1)}^{3} \\  & =(6x({x}^{3}-1)+36{x}^{4})\,{({x}^{3}-1)}^{3} \\  & =(6{x}^{4}-6x+36{x}^{4})\,{({x}^{3}-1)}^{3} \\  & =(42{x}^{4}-6x)\,{({x}^{3}-1)}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at $x=1$, we substitute $x=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})|}_{x=1} & =(42\cdot {1}^{4}-6\cdot 1){({1}^{3}-1)}^{3} \\  & =36\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{p}},
$$

where $p$ is a constant. The $p$-series test states that

- if $p>1,$ then the series converges, while

- if $p\le 1,$ then the series diverges.

Comparing our series to the $p$-series, we have

p=2q-2.
$$

$$

Therefore, the series is convergent for all $q>\frac{3}{2}.$

Which of the following series converge?

I. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}^{3}}}$

questions.worked_solution:
We analyze each series in turn.

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}^{3}}}={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{3/2}},
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{3}{2}.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{n}^{5}}}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{5/4}},
$$

 
which is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{5}{4}.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{\sqrt{{n}^{3}}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{{n}^{3/2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{1/2}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{1}{2}.$ Since $p\le 1,$ the series is divergent.

Hence, the correct answer is "I and II only".

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[
y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(x^{2} +2x - 2\right).
\]

Differentiating gives
\[
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (2x + 2).
\]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt]

&=\cos u \cdot \pi (2x+2)\\[5pt]

&=\pi (2x+2)\cos u\\[5pt]

&=\pi (2x+2)\cos \left(  \pi \left(x^{2} +2x - 2\right) \right).
\end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find

\begin{align}
f'(1) & =\pi (2\cdot1+2)\cos \left(  \pi \left(1^{2} +2\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\[3pt]

& =4\pi \cos(\pi) \\[3pt]
&= 4\pi \cdot (-1) \\[3pt]
&= -4\pi
\end{align}

Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
\[
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-4\pi}.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether an Ordinary Differential Equation is Autonomous or Nonautonomous
questions.problem:
Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

I. - ${y}^{'}-8{e}^{y}=2$
II. - $y{y}^{'}+3=\operatorname{cos}y$
III. - $x{y}^{'}-8={e}^{y}$
questions.worked_solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form ${y}^{'}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'}-8{e}^{y} & =2 \\ {y}^{'} & =8{e}^{y}+2 \\ {y}^{'} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=8{e}^{y}+2.$

- Equation II is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form ${y}^{'}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y{y}^{'}+3 & =\operatorname{cos}y \\ {y}^{'} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}y-3}{y} \\ {y}^{'} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}y-3}{y}.$

- Equation III is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{'}-8 & ={e}^{y} \\ {y}^{'} & =\frac{{e}^{y}+8}{x} \\ {y}^{'} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{y}+8}{x}.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether an Ordinary Differential Equation is Autonomous or Nonautonomous
questions.problem:
Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

I. - $x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{y}^{3}=2$
II. - $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-7{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{y}$
III. - $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{ln}y$
questions.worked_solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{y}^{3} & =2 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2+3{y}^{3}}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{2+3{y}^{3}}{x}.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

- Equation II is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-7{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =7{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=7{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{y}.$

- Equation III is an autonomous differential equation. We see that it is of the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ where $f(y)=\operatorname{ln}y.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

I. - ${e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{y}^{3}=0$
II. - $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x=\operatorname{ln}y$
III. - $5x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x}=0$
questions.worked_solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{y}^{3} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{y}^{3}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=3{y}^{3}{e}^{-y}.$

$$

$$

where $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}y+2x.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{5{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{5{x}^{2}}.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Given that  ${a}_{n}=4{n}^{6}$ for $n\ge 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. - $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1$
II. - ${a}_{n}$ is an increasing sequence
III. - ${a}_{n}$ is a decreasing sequence
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is a positive sequence defined for $n\ge 1,$ and that

$$
L=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}.
$$

Then,

- if $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *increasing,* and

- if $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *decreasing.*

Notice that, in this case, ${a}_{n}=4{n}^{6}$ is positive for all $n\ge 1.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement.

- Statement I is true. Computing the ratio $L,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}} \\  & =\frac{4(n+1)^{6}}{4{n}^{6}} \\  & =\frac{(n+1)^{6}}{{n}^{6}} \\  & ={(\frac{n+1}{n})}^{6} \\  & ={(\frac{n}{n}+\frac{1}{n})}^{6} \\  & ={(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $n\ge 1,$ we have that $\frac{1}{n}>0.$ Therefore, it follows that 

$$
(1+\frac{1}{n})>1,
$$

and therefore 

$$
L={(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{6}>1.
$$

- Statement II is true whereas statement III is false. Since $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ we can conclude that the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is increasing.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Sum to Infinity of a Geometric Series Given Two of Its Terms
questions.problem: Consider the positive infinite geometric sequence that has a first term equal to $100$ and a third term equal to $4.$ What is the sum to infinity of the terms of this sequence?
questions.worked_solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

From the question statement we have ${a}_{1}=100$ and ${a}_{3}=4.$ We can find the common ratio using the following formula:

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}
$$

Substituting in the known information into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3-1} & =\frac{4}{100} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{25} \\ r & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{25}} \\ r & =\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we have taken the positive square root since we're told that the sequence is positive.

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{100}{(1-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =\frac{100}{(\frac{4}{5})} \\  & =100\cdot \frac{5}{4} \\  & =125.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent, which of the following statements are true?

I. - $11\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent
II. - ${\sum }_{n=16}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent
III. - $11\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}+{\sum }_{n=16}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent
questions.worked_solution:

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Partial Sum of an Infinite Arithmetic Series
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=4n-1.$ If we compute the first few terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =3 \\ {a}_{2} & =7 \\ {a}_{3} & =11,\end{aligned}
$$

and we see that this is an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=4$ and ${a}_{1}=3.$

We can compute the $k$th partial sum of an arithmetic series using the formula

$$
{s}_{k}=\frac{k}{2}({a}_{1}+{a}_{k}).
$$

Since ${a}_{k}=4k-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{k} & =\frac{k}{2}(3+(4k-1)) \\  & =\frac{k}{2}(4k+2) \\  & =k(2k+1).\end{aligned}
$$
